A: For forty years, a puppet theater has used hand-painted cloth backdrops changed by visible stagehands. Digital projections would allow richer settings and attract younger audiences, but retiring the cloth would end a craft passed between generations of performers. Should the director introduce projected scenery or preserve the theater's traditional handmade staging?
B: Every spring, residents paint the neighborhood underpass together using brushes and a design chosen at a public picnic. A design firm offers a durable printed mural that can be installed in one day, though it would end the annual communal ritual. Should organizers accept the modern installation or continue the shared painting tradition?
C: An orchestra treasurer has saved ticket revenue to repair the only concert piano. A young guest musician loses her violin in a house fire and cannot afford a rental for next week's audition. Helping her would postpone the piano repair and cancel rehearsals. Should the treasurer protect the orchestra's reserve or fund the violin rental?

A: A boarding school has begun each day with students reading announcements aloud in the central hall for eighty years. A mobile bulletin would reach absent pupils and update instantly, but staff and alumni value gathering around the old lectern. Should the headteacher introduce the digital bulletin or preserve the morning reading tradition?
B: A programming team has always reviewed new code by gathering around one monitor every Friday afternoon. An asynchronous online system would include remote colleagues and shorten delays, but remove a ritual that shaped the company's collaborative culture. Should the team move reviews online or maintain the established Friday gathering?
C: A professor discovers that her closest colleague invented several student quotations in a published teaching study. Correcting the article would preserve an honest record but could end his appointment and damage a long friendship. Should she notify the journal about the fabricated evidence or shield the colleague who supported her during tenure review?

A: A vineyard still harvests its oldest field by hand during a three-day gathering of relatives and neighbors. A mechanical harvester would finish before forecast rain and reduce labor, but would end the annual practice through which younger family members learn the land. Should the owner adopt machine harvesting or preserve the communal hand-picked vintage?
B: A rowing club has selected crews through timed river trials since its founding. New indoor sensors could compare athletes more precisely throughout winter, yet members regard the river trial as a defining rite shared with earlier generations. Should coaches adopt continuous digital selection or retain the traditional race on the river?
C: A cooperative promises grocery stores its first strawberry shipment by Monday. Packing that quickly would require skipping a second inspection and sending some bruised fruit, while two more days would ensure every box meets the growers' standard but miss the launch promotion. Should the cooperative ship on Monday or delay delivery for better quality?

A: A family restaurant has served one fixed Sunday menu from the grandmother's handwritten recipes for sixty years. Introducing rotating regional dishes could draw new customers, but regulars and relatives consider the unchanged meal part of the family's continuity. Should the new owner redesign the menu or preserve the traditional Sunday service?
B: A primary school has taught local history through an annual walking tour led by retired residents. Interactive classroom archives would offer more sources and work in bad weather, yet the walk preserves a valued exchange between children and elders. Should teachers replace it with the digital course or keep the long-standing community tour?
C: A hardware shop owner has reserved cash to replace a delivery van that may fail soon. His longtime cashier needs an emergency deposit to escape an unsafe flat with her daughter. Lending the money could leave the shop unable to make deliveries. Should the owner protect the vehicle fund or help his employee move immediately?

A: A research institute removes anyone who misses two mandatory safety trainings from laboratory access. One technician missed the second session while caring for his wife during chemotherapy and asks to remain until the next course. Others lost access under the same rule. Should the director suspend him equally or grant an exception for his hardship?
B: A coding boot camp refunds tuition only when students withdraw during the first week. One participant asks for a late refund after becoming the sole carer for an injured parent, though earlier withdrawals received nothing. Returning her money would help with rent but break the known policy. Should the school enforce the deadline or show her mercy?
C: A planetary scientist is offered leadership of a celebrated observatory on another continent. The role would crown years of research and open major projects, but her partner cannot move and she would leave the close lab group that gathers at her home every week. Should she pursue the directorship or remain with the people who anchor her life?

A: A basketball league automatically suspends every player who receives three technical fouls. A teenager reaches the limit after shouting when he learned his brother had been hospitalized, and the suspension covers a final attended by scouts. Should officials apply the established penalty like they did for others or excuse him because of the crisis?
B: A field station charges all researchers who return equipment late because the next teams lose access. One graduate student was delayed rescuing an injured hiker and cannot afford the fee. Waiving it recognizes the emergency but treats her differently from previous late borrowers. Should the station collect the standard charge or make an exception?
C: A climbing coach can let trainees choose any route across a newly opened cliff, possibly discovering creative lines. A protected course with inspected anchors offers fewer surprises but sharply reduces uncertain falls and rescue delays. Should the coach permit free exploration of the cliff or require everyone to use the verified route?

A: A clinic cancels appointments when patients arrive more than fifteen minutes late, a rule applied throughout the year. An elderly man arrives twenty minutes late because his bus broke down and asks to be seen before his medication runs out. Should the receptionist enforce the same cancellation rule or grant him an exception because of his predicament?
B: A college requires every student who misses a final examination to provide medical documentation. One student missed it while protecting her younger siblings during a sudden eviction but has no official record. Others without documents were failed. Should the dean apply the requirement consistently or allow her a special examination because of the hardship?
C: A surgeon is invited to discuss her experience with panic attacks during a hospital mentoring session. Disclosure could help junior doctors speak honestly and create trust, but it would reveal a diagnosis she has kept from colleagues and patients. Should she share her personal history with the group or preserve that part of her privacy?

A: The housing authority removes applicants who miss a document deadline from the waiting list. One mother submits a day late after her child was hospitalized, while other late applicants have already been removed. Restoring her place would recognize a genuine crisis but depart from the published rule. Should the officer reject her application or make an exception?
B: A dental clinic charges the same missed-appointment fee to every patient. A factory worker fails to attend because an unexpected shift was the only way to avoid dismissal, and paying the fee would consume his grocery money. Should the manager apply the standard charge or waive it in response to his specific hardship?
C: A civil engineer can lead a nationally prominent bridge program if she relocates for three years. The appointment offers rapid promotion and recognition, but her aging parents, partner, and lifelong friends all live nearby and share frequent routines. Should she accept the career-making assignment or remain closely involved with the people she loves?

A: A community garden assigns plots to the next person on its waiting list whenever rent is fourteen days late. A gardener falls behind after paying for her son's emergency travel, although two earlier members lost plots under the same rule. Should the committee reassign her plot fairly or allow extra time because of her hardship?
B: A market requires every vendor to open by eight or surrender that day's stall. A florist arrives late after taking an injured neighbor to hospital, while previous late vendors were turned away. Letting her trade would prevent spoiled flowers but break equal treatment. Should the manager enforce the opening rule or grant her an exception?
C: A volunteer choir director wants to improve at the piano by practicing scales every evening for a year. Comfortable conversations at the local pub are immediately appealing, while the solitary drills promise only gradual skill later. Should he keep the demanding practice schedule or spend those evenings enjoying easier company?

A: A software founder is negotiating with employees who distrust her sudden absences. Explaining that she is undergoing fertility treatment could restore confidence and help them plan schedules together, but it would expose intimate information she intended to keep private. Should she disclose the reason for her absences or preserve her privacy despite the team's uncertainty?
B: A playwright is asked to tell actors that the central character draws directly from his estranged brother's addiction. Revealing this could help the cast understand difficult scenes and collaborate more honestly, but it would expose a painful family history. Should he share the personal source with the company or keep it confidential?
C: An app developer can substantially increase advertising revenue by recording users' locations every few minutes. The data would enrich her personally, but the extra tracking consumes energy across millions of phones and encourages more server use and electronic turnover. Should she adopt the profitable tracking system or accept less income to reduce its widespread costs?

A: A novelist joins a workshop whose members want to know why her manuscript portrays foster care so precisely. Telling them she grew up in care could build trust and lead to sharper feedback, but she has never shared that history publicly. Should she reveal the personal connection or keep her childhood private during the collaboration?
B: A professional runner is asked to tell teammates about the religious practice that limits when he can train. Sharing the details would help them coordinate and understand his choices, yet faith has always remained private for him. Should he explain the practice openly or protect his personal information while accepting continued confusion?
C: A stage manager develops a severe ear infection before the final weekend of a touring musical. The doctor recommends silence and rest, but she alone knows every lighting cue and the understudy has never run the full production. Should she stay home to recover or fulfill her responsibility to the cast and audience?

A: A lecturer notices students interpreting her extended leave as disinterest in their course. Explaining that she cared for a parent with dementia could rebuild trust and make communication more open, but it would reveal family circumstances she promised to keep private. Should she tell the class what happened or preserve her family's confidentiality?
B: A farm cooperative asks a new member to explain why she refuses overnight shifts during certain weeks. Disclosing her ongoing fertility treatment would help others schedule fairly and may create understanding, but exposes deeply personal medical information. Should she share the reason with the group or keep it private despite their suspicions?
C: An agricultural college has opened graduation with students leading decorated cattle through the town for a century. A modern indoor ceremony would be accessible in any weather, but alumni and farmers regard the procession as essential continuity. Should the college move graduation indoors or preserve the traditional cattle parade?
